title: Juliet Daniel changed cancer research. Students of the late Canadian scientist say she also changed lives
summary: Friends, students and colleagues gathered this week at McMaster University in Hamilton to celebrate Juliet Daniel, a Barbadian-Canadian professor and scientist who died April 28 at age 61. They…

image.caption: Juliet Daniel, a Barbadian-Canadian professor, scientist and community advocate, was 61 when she passed away on April 28. (Submitted by Juliet Daniel)

blocks.text: Shaiya Robinson saw something she hadn't seen before — a Black woman leading a cancer research lab — when she was a student and first met Juliet Daniel at McMaster University for an interview in 2009.
Robinson, who had rarely encountered Black professors, said the meeting to join the lab was about more than an interview. It was the first time she could picture herself in that position.
"I'd never had a Black professor before."
Daniel became her supervisor, mentor and, eventually, a colleague.
Now, Robinson is an assistant professor at McMaster, carrying forward many of the lessons she learned from the woman who helped make that future possible.

Robinson was among former students, friends and colleagues who gathered Monday at McMaster University to honour the legacy of Daniel. The Barbadian-Canadian professor and scientist was a longtime breast cancer survivor who died on April 28 at age 61.
"She was such a pivotal person in every step of my career journey and my personal journey," Robinson recalled.
Determined to ask different questions
Daniel joined McMaster in November 1999 as an assistant professor, becoming the first Black woman faculty member in the university's faculty of science.
Her research focused on understanding why certain cancers impact some populations more than others, and why outcomes can differ.
She was internationally recognized for her research into triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), an aggressive form of the disease that disproportionately affects Black and Hispanic women.

Her work helped advance understanding of the genetic differences behind cancer outcomes, including her discovery of a gene she named Kaiso, after a style of calypso music rooted in her Caribbean heritage.
Michele James knew Daniel for about 30 years and sits on the board of The Olive Branch of Hope (TOBOH), a breast cancer support organization.
James said Daniel was looking into health equity and reducing health-care disparities long before it became a mainstream conversation.
"She was a real trailblazer in that regard."

Daniel co-founded organizations including the African Caribbean Faculty Association of McMaster, the Canadian Black Scientists Network, the McMaster Academic Women’s Success and Mentorship Lecture Series, and the Canadian Multicultural LEAD Organization for Mentoring and Training. (Paul Smith/CBC)
Made time for students, community
Robinson said Daniel had a demanding schedule, but somehow always made students and colleagues feel they had her full attention.
"She didn't have time, but she always made you feel like there was time for you."
Daniel also mentored Kevin Kelly, who now works in biotechnology.

Kelly met Daniel in 2000, when he was an undergraduate student looking for a supervisor for his research project. He stayed in her lab through his PhD, becoming the first doctoral graduate from her research group.
Kelly said Daniel was someone who took mentorship seriously and was generous with her time.
"She was always thinking about her students."
He said he admired her willingness to pursue questions that drew little scientific attention, particularly around cancer in Black women.
Kevin Kelly and Dr. Shaiya Robinson, left to right, were both mentored by Daniel. They remember her for her scientific accomplishments and compassionate style of mentoring. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)

Daniel also helped build a stronger community for Black academics. She co-founded the African Caribbean Faculty Association of McMaster and the Canadian Black Scientists Network, along with several other initiatives supporting mentorship, inclusion and student success.

"I was really proud of her for taking that very courageous step," James said. "She was already busy and that was something else that she took on to help advance things not for herself, but for the other faculty members."
Proud to be Bajan
For Stephanie Roberts, Daniel was first and foremost a childhood friend.

The two grew up in the same neighbourhood in Barbados, meeting when Roberts was about three and Daniel was five. They remained close even after Daniel moved to Canada and Roberts immigrated to the United States.
Roberts recalled Daniel's determination to make a difference in cancer research, particularly after her mother died of the disease.
She said Daniel initially pursued medicine before choosing research as a way to help find better answers for people affected by cancer.
"It was never about the money," Roberts said. "She truly wanted a cure for cancer."

items: To confront race in Canada, she became a beauty queen, a tour guide and a time traveller

blocks.text: Although they were in different job fields, Daniel would sometimes invite Roberts to tag along on work trips.
She also remembers Daniel as a longtime friend from her home country.
Daniel loved calypso music, dancing, cooking and hosting friends, and was an accomplished ballroom dancer who won several awards, Roberts said.
She said Daniel never made a point of introducing herself by her title, despite her academic achievements.
"If you went anywhere with her, she always went and said, 'Hi, I'm Juliet.'"
Pioneering cancer researcher wants more diversity in STEM fields
Roberts says Daniel was always proud to be from Barbados and would do whatever she could to give back.
James said Daniel helped the island during the COVID-19 pandemic by connecting its government with people who could facilitate access to vaccines, medical expertise and supplies.

Daniel's contributions earned her numerous honours, including being named a Distinguished University Professor in 2025, McMaster's highest recognition for faculty members. Her research has been cited more than 6,400 times.
In 2024, the federal government's Canadian Intellectual Property Office named Daniel as one of three Black Innovators in Research and Medicine.
Roberts hopes Daniel's name will be permanently recognized, including at a potential tribute at McMaster and possibly seeing Barbados's living lab named after her.
"It's just sad that in most cases, we have to wait on some till someone passes to celebrate them."
Robinson said she wants to continue Daniel's example by making mentorship a priority for her own students.
The event to honour Daniel drew friends, colleagues, students and mentees to the McLean Centre for Collaborative Discovery at McMaster University. (Jeffery Tram/CBC)
During Monday's celebration, James shared a quote that she said captured Daniel's approach to life: "It's better to light one small candle than to curse the darkness."
James noted that the celebration drew many people whose lives were touched by Daniel.
"She was like a candle that you can just take that candle and use it to light lots and lots of other candles," she said.
"And as I looked out into the room this afternoon, I felt that there were so many candles that had been lit initially by Juliet, and that their light would carry on indefinitely."
